title: The king and the palanquin bearer
hook: a king mocks his bearer for looking weak, and the bearer answers that tired and thin belong to the body, earth carrying earth
carry: parinama: the body changes; the seer doesn't
tomorrow: Vyasa sees the hard days coming

segments.voice: Yesterday: prajna, and your line, samyama: the three, held on one thing, the way Ekalavya held one image and one target, day after day.
screen: `SAMYAMA: THE THREE, HELD ON ONE THING.`

segments.voice: A king named Rahugana is being carried across the country in a palanquin, on his way to learn wisdom from the sage Kapila. One bearer is missing, so the servants grab a strong-looking stranger off the road. He is Bharata, a great soul who looks like a simpleton. He walks carefully, eyes on the ground ahead, so he won't step on any small creature, and the palanquin lurches. The king leans out and mocks him. Poor fellow, you must be so tired. Carried it all alone, have you? Not very stout, are you?
screen: `A KING IN A PALANQUIN.` → `A BEARER WATCHING FOR ANTS.` → `'NOT VERY STOUT, ARE YOU?'`

segments.voice: Bharata answers, calmly. Everything you said is true, of the body. Fat, thin, tired: those belong to it, not to me. Then he takes the whole scene apart. On the earth are feet. On the feet, legs, a waist, shoulders. On the shoulders, a wooden palanquin. In it sits someone called a king. All of it is earth, in different shapes, carrying earth. The king climbs down and falls at his feet. That's the Bhagavata Purana, and it carries one of Hinduism's central teachings: you are not the body. The body is changing earth; the self, the atman, watches the change and doesn't change. Patanjali maps the change itself. The word is parinama, transformation. Sutra 3.9: even a mind growing still is changing. Sutra 3.13: everything changes in property, in time and in condition. Sutra 3.14 names what stays underneath, the substance that carries the change. The classical commentary's example is clay: a lump becomes a pot, the pot breaks into shards, the shards become dust, and the clay is there the whole way through. And in the Yoga Sutras' wider picture, the seer itself doesn't change at all. Only the seen does. Why put this in a book on meditation? To rest the mind on anything, you have to see clearly what changes and what carries the change. And it's an old Hindu comfort. A face in a photo from ten years ago, a grandparent whose hands have grown thin: the forms keep changing. The one looking out through them doesn't.
screen: `FAT, THIN, TIRED: THE BODY'S, NOT MINE.` · `EARTH CARRYING EARTH.` · `PARINAMA: PROPERTY, TIME, CONDITION.` · `CLAY: LUMP, POT, SHARDS, DUST.` · then, large: `THE BODY CHANGES; THE SEER DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: Rest on the breath and watch a thought arise, stay a moment and fade, then the next, without following its story. Notice sensations in the body rising and fading too. Then notice what doesn't seem to rise and fade, the watching itself, and stay with that for a few breaths.
Parinama, change of form. Bodies, minds, even stillness change, carried by something that stays.
Your line: parinama: the body changes; the seer doesn't. Earth carrying earth, and someone watching. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindus learn early, from the Gita and from stories like Bharata's, that the self is not the body; students of the Yoga Sutras study the transformations of 3.9–3.15 with the classical commentary, and in meditation watch thoughts and sensations arise and fade.

fork.setup: you're holding a lump of clay. it becomes a pot, then breaks into shards. what has changed?
options: the form and stage; the clay is still there.
fork.reveal: the commentary's example: lump, pot, shards, dust. properties come and go; the substance that carries them stays (3.14–3.15).

original.note: Sanskrit pariṇāma: transformation, change of form; three kinds in 3.9–3.12 and three more in 3.13.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation stops the mind from changing.
what it means: body and mind change in property, time and condition, while the self that watches doesn't, which is what Bharata told the king.
what a scholar hears: nirodha-, samadhi- and ekagrata-parinama (3.9–3.12); dharma-, lakshana- and avastha-parinama (3.13); the Bhashya's clay; Bharata's earth upon earth to Rahugana (Bhagavata 5.12).
recall: resting upon: following after a memory

a ritual that turns clay into a sacred pot
